cost_basis: run log of docs/RESULTS.md plus per-answer cost of experiments

anchors.name: TypeSafe-style typed decisions
anchors.source: third-party write-up of Jev on the typed-decisions benchmark (see JEV-AND-LAYA-KNOWLEDGE.md section 7)

anchors.name: Banking77 (77 intents)
anchors.source: spread of eight independent Jev runs collected in docs/RESULTS.md section 2, point 2

tests.name: Smoke test
tests.asks: Do Choice, Score and Noul answers work end to end?
tests.result: All three answer types were returned and parsed with 0 errors.

tests.name: Anchors and baselines
tests.asks: Does this harness reproduce published numbers, and what do well-known sets give?
tests.result: Banking77 80.7%, SST-2 97.0%, BoolQ 92.0%, MMLU-Pro 82.7%, MedMCQA 73.0%, SMS spam 98.0%.

tests.name: Numbers control (ULB)
tests.asks: Can Jev read anonymous numbers, such as card transactions?
tests.result: 50.0% on a 50/50 set: chance. It says 'not fraud' to every item.

tests.name: Question or statement
tests.asks: Does phrasing the yes/no as a question or as a statement change the answer?
tests.result: BoolQ 89.0% vs 91.0%; SMS spam 99.0% vs 99.0%; SST-2 97.0% vs 97.0%: no real difference.

tests.name: Core business domains
tests.asks: How good is Jev on one strong, human-labelled dataset per business domain?

tests.name: Stress tests and calibration
tests.asks: Reasoning, negation, perturbed text, long documents, 200 options, and agreement with human raters.

tests.name: Numbers or words for severity levels
tests.asks: Is Jev's weakness on CVSS severity caused by number ranges in the wording, or by the task?
tests.result: 52.2% with numbers, 49.7% in words (p = 0.16): the task is the problem.

tests.name: Number of options
tests.asks: How does accuracy change with 4, 6, 16, 32 and 64 options on the same items?
tests.result: From 4 to 64 options Jev lost 2 to 21 points on 6 datasets and stayed 49 to 61 times above chance.

tests.name: Failure-mode probes
tests.asks: Padding, a negated question, an injected instruction, and contradictory definitions.
tests.result: Robust to all four on the three tasks tested; see the failure-mode scorecard.

tests.name: Decomposition
tests.asks: Is one hard question worse than several narrow ones combined?
tests.result: Phishing: 83.3% with one question, 92.3% with six narrow questions combined (p = 0.0001).

tests.name: A 'none of these' option
tests.asks: Does an explicit way to abstain beat simply dropping low-confidence answers?
tests.result: Jev abstains on 0.0% to 4.0% of items and the option adds nothing over a confidence cut-off.

tests.name: Question format
tests.asks: Do batching 28 questions, reversing the option order or renaming the option keys change the answers?
tests.result: Same pick on 99.5% of answers when batched; option order and key names change no dataset significantly.

A.label: Works as-is
A.rule: Accuracy at least 85%, removes at least half of the always-majority baseline's errors, and at most 3% of all answers are wrong with confidence 0.9 or more.

B.label: Works with a cut-off or review
B.rule: Not A, and accuracy at least 70% while removing at least a quarter of the baseline's errors, or (yes/no questions) ROC-AUC at least 0.90, so a per-task cut-off or human review would work.

C.label: Not usable zero-shot
C.rule: Anything else: fine-tune, redesign the question, or use another tool.

open_questions: Double negatives written into the evidence text.
True multi-hop question answering over several documents.
Scoping words and implied conditions, with a dedicated test.
P(q) + P(not q) across different questions on the same state.
Other injection styles, such as an end marker or an instruction hidden inside a retrieved document.
More than 64 options in a controlled test (the real label sets of 100 to 200 options were measured).
A re-run on a newer Jev version (the public Hugging Face index already uses jev-1.14.0; this run used jev-1.13.0).
